title: Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed
full_review:
Zoinks! Those "meddling kids" are at it again in the lackluster comedy "Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed" (Warner Brothers).

Like its 2002 predecessor, the sequel stays true to its cartoon roots. However, this second installment rarely progresses past the first film's self-conscious parodying style, resulting in an overwrought movie full of forced, retread humor. Thankfully, director Raja Gosnell (who also directed the original) has, at least, toned down the age-inappropriate innuendo and spring-break ambiance that rattled the chains of some parents last time around.

For those pop-culturally illiterate few, the framework of the TV show was quite simple: Each episode involved a quartet of self-fashioned sleuths collectively known as "Mystery Inc." exposing some bump-in-the-night being as an all-too-human fraud. Returning for another spin in the psychedelic mystery machine are the film's four leads -- Freddie Prinze Jr. as fearless leader Fred; Sarah Michelle Gellar as the Barbie-doll Buffy, oops, Daphne; Linda Cardellini as Velma, the bespectacled brains behind the operation; and Matthew Lillard as everyone's favorite lily-livered, chronically famished scruffmeister, Shaggy. Neil Fanning also repeats as the voice of Scooby-Doo, the team's computer-generated Great Dane mascot (admirably filling the dog collar of legendary Hanna-Barbera vocal artist Don Messick).

In the film, Mystery Inc. is riding high as Coolville's most celebrated crime-solving clique. The curtain rises as they arrive at the red carpet opening of a new exhibit of their greatest cases.
But the festivities are interrupted when the party is crashed -- literally -- by a giant flying beaked lizard known as Pterodactyl Ghost, prompting one of the movie's few witty lines, "How did that dinosaur get through security?" A sinister masked figure shows up announcing more monsters are on the way, including the 10,000 Volt Ghost and the Skelemen. Mystery Inc. immediately goes into sleuthing mode -- all, that is except for Shaggy and Scoobs who dive into their usual hiding place underneath the nearest available piece of furniture.

Can the gang stop the enigmatic impresario and his monster-making machine, or will the madman succeed in transforming Coolsville into Ghoulsville?

A crusty Peter Boyle plays Old Man Winkles, who had once donned the disguise of the fiendish Black Knight Ghost and who the team thinks is now responsible for the outbreak of paranormal pandemonium. Or could the bogeyman be Patrick Wesley (Seth Green), the love-struck curator of the crime museum, who has the intimacy-averse Velma's tangerine sweater all tied in knots? Further complicating matters is the relentless hounding of TV reporter Heather Jasper-Howe (Alicia Silverstone), who seems hell bent on besmirching the reputation of the home town heroes.
Trying to graft some psychological depth onto the cartoon cadre, Gosnell concocts a silly subplot involving Shaggy and Scooby in which they renounce their fraidy-cat ways and vow to be less "lametastical" -- though choosing to be part of this "lame" affair is hardly getting off on the right foot -- or paw. The only thought that should occupy Scooby's mind is where and when he will receive his next Scooby snack.

During their investigation, Velma discovers that many of the assorted miscreants have been created from "randomonium," an invented substance whose designation on the periodic table of elements would probably be "NF" -- as in "not funny." Of course, "randomonium" is what the film is made out of as well, since the nonsensical script is a collection of "random" bloated special-effects sequences that add up to very little in terms of narrative coherence, and even less in terms of entertainment. For parents concerned about bringing easily frightened children, the assorted ghouls rank, for the most part, very low on the creep-o-meter.

And while the film imparts a light message about self-acceptance and teamwork, the rickety script and cardboard characters make the original animated series look downright Shakespearean by comparison; at least as cartoons, they had an excuse for being so two-dimensional.

In one scene, Shaggy, having just survived a close call with a spooky specter, informs his friends that he is OK -- "if you define OK as massive agony." Using Shaggy's definition, one could say that watching this film is, well, "OK."

Due to some mild crude language and puerile humor, as well as some scary action sequences, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
